query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In an equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy, introducing a minor substitution of approximately 10 atomic percent Sn (to form, for example, a FeCoNiSn alloy with near-equiatomic proportions) will induce a partial transformation from the initial single-phase FCC structure to a dual-phase microstructure with a controlled BCC fraction. This mixed FCC+BCC microstructure is expected to increase the magnetocrystalline anisotropy and promote enhanced domain wall pinning, thereby increasing the coercivity by roughly a factor of 2–3 compared to the baseline FeCoNi alloy or its Pd/Pt derivatives.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline material is an as-cast, equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting a homogeneous single-phase FCC structure with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 10 atomic percent Sn into the system, resulting in an alloy composed of roughly equal parts Fe, Co, Ni, and Sn. Process the alloy via conventional casting followed by controlled thermal annealing.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be synthesized under conditions that maintain high configurational entropy (≥ 1.0R) and then annealed at temperatures in the 600–700 K range for sufficient time (e.g., 1 hour) to facilitate the controlled nucleation of the BCC phase without excessive coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure wherein a controlled fraction (targeting approximately 20–30% by volume) of the alloy adopts a BCC structure distributed as fine precipitates within the predominant FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The minor addition of Sn destabilizes the pure FCC phase, fostering a partial transformation to a BCC structure that exhibits higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The nanoscale BCC precipitates act as domain wall pinning centers, impeding domain wall propagation and thereby increasing the coercivity relative to the baseline soft magnetic behavior of the pure FCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified FeCoNiSn high-entropy alloy will display a significantly increased coercivity—estimated to be 2–3 times higher than that of the baseline FeCoNi alloy—while maintaining a high saturation magnetization. This enhanced coercivity should make the material more suitable for applications requiring stronger resistance to demagnetization, compared to the softer ferromagnetic behavior of the FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the conventional equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy (or its derivatives with Pd/Pt), which exhibit low coercivity due to a single-phase FCC structure with high saturation magnetization.
generation.boundary: This intervention is effective provided that the Sn content and annealing conditions are optimized to achieve only a partial FCC-to-BCC transformation. Excessive BCC phase formation might lead to a significant reduction in saturation magnetization or other undesired magnetic properties. The approach applies primarily at processing temperatures where phase transformation kinetics are favorable (around 600–700 K).
generation.uncertainty: Key uncertainties include the exact Sn concentration needed to achieve the optimal balance between FCC and BCC phases, the sensitivity of coercivity enhancement to annealing time and temperature, and potential trade-offs between increased coercivity and any changes in saturation magnetization or remanence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and a second set where approximately 10 atomic percent of Sn is substituted (resulting in an equiatomic or near-equiatomic FeCoNiSn composition). Use identical casting procedures followed by annealing at 600–700 K for 1 hour. Characterize the phase composition using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to quantify the presence of any BCC phase and use vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) to measure the hysteresis loops, focusing on coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification (XRD) to assess the FCC/BCC phase fraction.
Magnetic hysteresis curves (VSM) to measure coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-substituted samples do not show a statistically significant (e.g., >25%) increase in coercivity relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy, or if the saturation magnetization is adversely reduced beyond acceptable levels compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

Zuo et al. [] found CoNiMnGa HEA shows a low saturation magnetostriction coefficient and a high Curie temperature (Tc). In our previous work [], the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA consisting of BCC and FCC phases shows good magnetic and mechanical properties, and it was found that BCC phases show a higher Ms than that of FCC phases for the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The other work of our group [] found a minor amount of Ga addition into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA can promote the formation of BCC phase and improve the Ms of the alloy, and the value of remanence (Br) and coercivity (Hc) also increases. It was reported that the addition of Sn can hinder the formation of FCC phase [] and promote the formation of BCC phase []. Therefore, in this work, a minor amount of Sn was added into the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA hoping to get a higher volume fraction of BCC phase. In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were studied from phase constitutions to microstructure and magnetic properties. It was found that these HEAs show high Ms, low Br, and high Tc, which indicate their potential application as soft magnetic materials. This paper offers a good method for designing future high-performance soft magnet

When the grain size is almost the same, the change trend of Hc may be related to Ms and K1 from this equation. When Ms reaches the maximum, the coercivity has the minimum value. In addition, the abnormal change of magnetic properties (Ms, Hc and Mr) at 7T may be related to the precipitated BCC phase. In the SMMs, high Ms, low Hc and low Mr are excellent results for use. In short, the magnetic behaviors of FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 HEA are improved by the solidification under the magnetic field, and the soft magnetic properties of the alloy are further optimized.

papers.title: Effect of Solidification on Microstructure and Properties of FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 High-Entropy Alloy Under Strong Static Magnetic Field.
papers.approach: Solidification processing under a strong static magnetic field (up to 7T) to tune the microstructure and magnetic properties
papers.findings: The study found that when solidified under a magnetic field the alloy remains as a single FCC phase and exhibits improved soft magnetic properties such as an increased saturation magnetization, lower yield strength, and minimum coercivity values (e.g., ~2.2 Oe at 5T). However, these improvements lead to even softer magnetic behavior rather than an increase in coercivity.
papers.mechanism: The magnetic field affects microstructural evolution (including possible formation of a minor BCC phase or precipitates at high fields) altering parameters like grain size, Ms, and anisotropy; yet the maximum Ms coincides with the lowest coercivity, indicating that enhanced ferromagnetic exchange (and high Ms) minimizes pinning of the domain walls.

papers.title: Magnetic Properties and Microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: FeCoNi-based alloy modified by a CuAl sublattice with minor Sn addition
papers.approach: Introducing a small amount of Sn (x from 0 to 0.10) into the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 alloy to promote phase changes
papers.findings: With increasing Sn content, the alloy shows an increase in saturation magnetization, coercivity, and hysteresis losses along with a decreasing trend in initial and maximum permeability. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of the BCC phase (and affects the morphology of Cu-rich nano-precipitates) while partially retaining the FCC phase.
papers.mechanism: The intervention is proposed to induce a phase transformation from the low-coercivity FCC phase to a mixture with an increasing BCC fraction. This phase change is expected to enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy and consequently increase the pinning of domain walls, thereby boosting coercivity.

established: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys typically possess a face‐centered cubic structure with high saturation magnetization and inherently low coercivity, making them effective soft magnets.

Utilizing strong static magnetic fields during solidification can modulate microstructure and magnetic parameters, though it tends to optimize soft magnetic properties rather than increasing coercivity.
Minor alloying additions can trigger phase transformations (e.g., FCC to BCC) in high-entropy systems, which in turn can influence magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain wall pinning.

approaches_tried.approach: Substitution with noble metals (Pd, Pt) in FeCoNi-based HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced alloys that remained soft ferromagnets with low coercivity despite the increased configurational complexity.

approaches_tried.approach: Solidification under strong static magnetic fields
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced aspects of soft magnetic performance (e.g., higher saturation magnetization and improved electrical resistivity) but led to lower coercivity.

approaches_tried.approach: Minor substitution (Sn addition) in the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 system
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased coercivity along with changes in phase fractions (enhancement of the BCC phase) that suggest improved domain wall pinning.

mechanisms: Phase transformation effects: Transition from a pure FCC structure to a mixed FCC/BCC structure increases magnetocrystalline anisotropy and hinders domain wall motion, thereby raising coercivity.

Microstructural modification by processing (e.g., magnetic-field-assisted solidification) can align or refine features that modulate magnetic behavior, though high saturation magnetization may counterintuitively reduce coercivity.
Minor alloying can alter nano-scale precipitate morphology and phase distribution, affecting magnetic domain interactions and pinning.
disagreements: While processing under a strong magnetic field improves overall soft magnetic performance, it does not address the need for higher coercivity, as the increase in Ms tends to correlate with lower Hc.

Some studies report that certain substitutions (e.g., Ga in FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 alloys) increase both remanence and coercivity, whereas Sn addition increases coercivity at the expense of remanence, indicating a trade-off that must be balanced.
open_questions: What is the optimal concentration and choice of substituent element (such as Sn) that maximizes coercivity without severely compromising other magnetic parameters?
Can the FCC to BCC phase transformation be controlled reliably in an equiatomic, high-entropy environment while maintaining the required entropy (≥ 1.0R)?
How do processing conditions or additional subtle alloying interventions interact with substitution to further enhance coercivity?
opportunities: Investigate minor doping strategies—such as small Sn additions—in FeCoNi-based HEAs to deliberately induce a controlled partial transition to a higher-anisotropy BCC phase; this offers a promising single intervention to increase coercivity relative to the baseline.

Evaluate combinations of low-concentration element additions with tailored processing (e.g., post-solidification thermal treatments) to optimize phase fractions and domain wall pinning, thereby providing a route to design FeCoNi-based alloys with enhanced coercivity.

Perform discriminating experiments to compare a baseline FeCoNi-based alloy against one with, for instance, 0.05–0.10 Sn substitution to identify the precise impact on coercivity and related magnetic properties under application-relevant conditions.

directions.direction: Minor elemental substitution with Sn to induce a controlled partial phase transformation from FCC to BCC.
directions.assessment: This approach leverages previous observations that small amounts of Sn in FeCoNi-based systems promote the formation of a BCC phase, which carries higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy and thus more effectively pins domain walls to yield higher coercivity. It directly addresses the limitation (low coercivity) while remaining in an almost equiatomic, high-entropy regime (entropy ≥ 1.0R). The underlying physics of phase stability and domain wall pinning is well established, and the strategy has been demonstrated in related systems (see PMC7512446::web::000::abstract and PMC7512446::web::002::1_introduction). The study is highly feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Minor substitution with Ga to subtly modify phase stability and precipitate morphology.
directions.assessment: Similar in concept to Sn addition, Ga can influence the volume fraction of the BCC phase and alter nano‐scale precipitate distribution. However, trade-offs between remanence and coercivity, and less straightforward effects compared to Sn, make this a less direct intervention. Feasible but may require more extensive compositional screening.

directions.direction: Tailored post-solidification thermal annealing to induce nano‐precipitates that act as domain wall pinning centers.
directions.assessment: A heat treatment schedule could induce subtle phase separation or nano‐structuring that impede domain wall motion. This method is supported by standard metallurgy practices, yet its effects on high-entropy systems can be complicated by diffusion kinetics. It is feasible and informative but may not be as directly controllable as a compositional modification.

directions.direction: Severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion) to refine the microstructure and introduce high density of defects for increased pinning.
directions.assessment: While grain refinement and defect incorporation can increase coercivity by hindering domain wall movement, past work indicates that such processing often leads to reduced coercivity in these high-entropy alloys due to enhanced soft magnetic exchange if not controlled carefully. The mechanism is known but may not be as effective in this context.

directions.direction: Surface oxidation to form a core–shell structure where an oxide layer on ferromagnetic cores enhances effective anisotropy.
directions.assessment: Inducing a native oxidation layer (or deliberate oxidation) can modify the magnetic anisotropy and domain wall dynamics. However, previous work shows that while core–shell structures improve resistivity and high-frequency behavior, they do not reliably produce higher coercivity over the baseline soft magnetic state. Thus, this approach is less directly aligned with the goal.

choice.why: This method most directly targets the low coercivity issue by promoting a controlled FCC-to-BCC phase transformation, thereby increasing magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain wall pinning. The intervention respects the high-entropy and near-equiatomic constraints and is supported by previous studies (e.g., PMC7512446::web::000::abstract, PMC7512446::web::002::1_introduction). It is also experimentally accessible and provides a clear, falsifiable pathway to enhance coercivity relative to the baseline FeCoNi alloy.
